newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs' bid to file Dow Corning plan denied.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs' bid to file Dow Corning plan denied.

text.p: In a blow to breast implant plaintiffs, Dow Corning Corp. said a federal bankruptcy judge on Monday denied the plaintiffs' bid to submit their own reorganization plan for the former implant maker.

U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Arthur Spector ruled that he will exclusively consider Dow Corning's own reorganization plan shortly after he rules on how damage claims in the case should be resolved. That decision was not expected until after mid-June.

Dow Corning was seeking to avoid paying thousands of claims that its silicone-gel breast implants caused connective-tissue diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis in women. It has offered to pay $600 million for claims of rupture and local complications in surrounding breast tissue.
Dow Corning, a joint venture between Dow Chemical Co. and Corning Inc. filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in May 1995 because of a crush of breast implant litigation.

The Midland, Mich.-based company has proposed that Spector hold a single trial to decide the controversial issue of whether the silicone implants cause disease, which is critical to valuing the claims. Plaintiffs have proposed that several such trials be held in state courts around the country.

On Monday, Spector advised attorneys of his confidential proposal for resolving the claims issue, and asked them to respond with comments by June 2. After he rules on the issue, Dow Corning will have 21 days to submit a new plan of reorganization, company spokesman T. Michael Jackson said.
Dow Corning officials hailed Monday's ruling as an important step in moving the two-year-old bankruptcy case toward resolution.
"Judge Spector recognized the extremely disruptive prospect of simultaneously allowing competing plans to move forward at this time," Dow Corning President Gary Anderson said in a statement.

"We intend to use this period to continue serious negotiations toward a fair resolution of this controversy. By focusing all parties on a single plan, we believe that this case can move forward more quickly so that legitimate claims can be fairly compensated."
Attorneys for the plaintiffs could not immediately be reached late on Monday.
In New Orleans on Monday, testimony continued in a breast implant trial naming Dow Chemical as a defendant, despite a federal appeals court ruling that such cases should be consolidated in Detroit.
Orleans Parish Civil Judge Yada McGee said she would not halt the trial until she is ordered to by U.S. District Judge Denise Hood in Detroit, who has been assigned the consolidated cases.
